title: Pydantic is all you need: Jason Liu

primary.label: Prompting & LLM Programming
primary.rationale: The talk's central thesis is structured prompting: representing LLM output contracts as typed Pydantic models rather than fragile string prompts. It systematically covers JSON schema generation, structured output patterns, classical and LLM-powered validators, retry-on-validation-error, escape-hatch schemas, reusable chain-of-thought components, and LLM-as-program patterns where data models carry execute methods. The taxonomy inclusion criteria for prompting_llm_programming states 'Primary focus is prompts, structured generation, or LLM-as-program patterns' with example topics 'structured output' and 'JSON schema', which directly match this talk's core content.

secondary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
secondary.rationale: The Instructor library is presented as a developer SDK that patches the OpenAI completion API to return guaranteed typed objects. The talk demonstrates infrastructure that other engineers build on—response_model parameter, nested model support, retry mechanisms. Taxonomy example topics 'SDK' and 'developer platform' apply, though the talk emphasizes patterns and methodology over the tool itself.

secondary.label: Tools, Protocols & Integrations
secondary.rationale: OpenAI function calling is the integration mechanism underlying the entire approach. The talk bridges function calling's raw dictionary outputs to typed Python objects via Pydantic. However, function calling is a means rather than the primary subject—the focus is on the structured output patterns built on top of it.

secondary.label: Retrieval, Search & Knowledge
secondary.rationale: The latter half demonstrates RAG with multi-backend search dispatch modeled as Pydantic objects, query decomposition into DAG nodes with dependencies, and knowledge graph extraction. These are substantial retrieval-focused demonstrations but are presented as applications of the structured prompting methodology rather than the primary focus.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The Instructor library and Pydantic-based structured prompting patterns are tools and methodologies used by software builders constructing LLM applications. The talk is explicitly aimed at developers building production LLM systems.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The structured prompting patterns, validators, escape-hatch schemas, and graph extraction techniques are domain-agnostic and applicable across any vertical using LLMs for structured output.

domains.label: Search & Knowledge
domains.rationale: RAG with multi-backend search, query decomposition, knowledge graph extraction, and citation-validated QA are demonstrated as concrete application patterns in the talk's second half.

summary: Jason Liu presents "Pydantic is all you need" at the inaugural AI Engineer Summit (October 8-10, 2023, San Francisco). His central thesis is that most production LLM applications are structured-output extraction problems, not chatbots, yet the common approach of prompting models for JSON strings and parsing with regex is fragile and unmanageable. He introduces Pydantic — a widely-trusted Python validation library with 70M monthly downloads — as the bridge between LLM function calling and typed Python code. Pydantic provides type-coerced data models, JSON schema generation, field validators, and IDE autocomplete, making prompts themselves become code rather than triple-quoted strings. Liu then demonstrates his Instructor library, which patches the OpenAI completion API so callers receive guaranteed Pydantic object instances via a response_model parameter. Key design patterns include: classical and LLM-powered field validators with max-retries that feeds validation errors back to the model for self-correction; escape-hatch schemas (MaybeUser) with optional result/error fields for uncertainty handling; reusable chain-of-thought components toggleable between testing and production; and graph/network extraction using ID-reference patterns to pull relational structures from unstructured text. In the latter half, Liu frames structured prompting as analogous to the shift from C to C++ — object-oriented development for LLM systems — where models output traversable data structures (graphs, DAGs, plans) that classical computer systems process. He demonstrates RAG with multiple search backends modeled as Pydantic objects with execute methods, query planning as a DAG with dependencies enabling parallel execution, knowledge graph extraction mirroring visualization APIs in ~40 lines of code, and citation-validated QA where fact quotes are validated as substrings against source text to prevent hallucination programmatically. He closes with future directions: multimodal structured outputs (bounding boxes, generative UI) and structured evaluation tooling.
whyItMatters: The software engineering concepts and AI concepts in this talk form a tightly coupled framework: structured prompting (the AI thesis) is operationalized through Pydantic typed data models (the SE foundation). JSON schema generation connects Python type definitions to LLM-consumable schemas, making prompts become code. Classical and LLM-powered validators enforce both syntactic and semantic constraints on model output, while the retry-on-validation-error pattern turns failures into self-correction loops. Escape-hatch schemas and toggleable chain-of-thought components address production concerns (uncertainty handling and latency). The more advanced patterns — graph extraction via ID references, polymorphic dispatch via execute methods, DAG query planning, and citation-validated QA — demonstrate that the same SE principle (typed data models with behavior) unlocks fundamentally new AI capabilities: LLMs outputting traversable data structures that classical systems process. The C-to-C++ analogy ties it together: just as OOP brought structure to procedural code, typed Pydantic models bring structure to LLM outputs, shifting the discipline from prompt engineering toward domain modeling. The Instructor library is the concrete tooling that makes this entire stack practical by patching the OpenAI API to guarantee typed responses.
temporalContext: This talk was presented live at the inaugural AI Engineer Summit on October 8-10, 2023, in San Francisco, and published to YouTube on November 1, 2023. At this time, OpenAI's function calling API (released June 2023) was the primary mechanism for structured output, and the dedicated Structured Outputs API feature would not be announced until August 6, 2024 — nearly a year later. Pydantic had approximately 70 million monthly downloads (confirmed plausible by first-party data showing 40M in Feb 2023 growing to 550M by Feb 2026). The Instructor library was relatively new (first GitHub release ~June 2023) but already gaining traction. The talk represents an early, influential articulation of the structured prompting paradigm, before it became a platform-level API feature at OpenAI. The video has accumulated 170K+ views, indicating sustained community interest.
takeaways: Most production LLM applications are structured-output extraction problems, not chatbots, yet JSON parsing from raw strings is unreliable and unmanageable.
Pydantic provides typed validation, autocomplete, and JSON schema output, making it the ideal bridge between LLM function calling and Python code.
The Instructor library patches OpenAI's API so responses are guaranteed Pydantic object instances with full type safety and nested model support.
Validators can be classical or LLM-powered, and max-retries feeds errors back to the model for automatic correction.
Structured prompting is analogous to the C-to-C++ shift: object-oriented development for LLM systems, enabling reuse, modularity, and methods on data models.
LLMs can output data structures—graphs, DAGs, plans—that classical computer systems traverse and process, replacing fragile agent loops.
RAG systems benefit from modeling searches, query decomposition, and multi-backend dispatch as Pydantic objects with execute methods.
Citation-validated QA uses validators to enforce that fact quotes exist as substrings in source text, preventing hallucination programmatically rather than through prompting.
Modeling data structures to mirror downstream APIs (e.g., graph visualization) yields dramatically simpler integration code.
Future directions include multimodal structured outputs (bounding boxes, generative UI over images/audio) and structured evaluation tooling.

concepts.name: Structured prompting
concepts.explanation: The practice of defining LLM output contracts as typed schemas (via Pydantic models) rather than free-text or raw JSON string prompts. Liu argues this unifies code quality, prompt quality, and data quality into a single maintainable artifact, shifting the discipline from prompt engineering toward domain modeling.
concepts.importance: Central organizing thesis of the talk; it reframes LLM application development from ad-hoc prompt crafting to software engineering with typed contracts.

concepts.name: OpenAI function calling
concepts.explanation: OpenAI's API feature that improves JSON placement in model responses. Liu notes it helps but still yields raw dictionaries requiring json.loads, leaving developers with unsafe, untyped data. The Instructor library builds on function calling to guarantee typed Pydantic objects.
concepts.importance: The integration mechanism underlying the entire approach; function calling is the API layer that Instructor patches to deliver structured output.

concepts.name: LLM-powered validators (llm_validator)
concepts.explanation: Validators that use an LLM to evaluate whether model output meets semantic constraints, rejecting malicious or inappropriate answers with natural-language error messages. This extends validation beyond syntactic checks to semantic quality enforcement.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that validation itself can be AI-powered, enabling enforcement of subjective or contextual constraints that classical validators cannot express.

concepts.name: Object-oriented LLM development (C-to-C++ analogy)
concepts.explanation: Liu frames structured prompting as analogous to the shift from C to C++: just as object-oriented programming brought structure to procedural code, typed Pydantic models bring structure to LLM outputs. LLMs can output data structures representing knowledge, workflows, and plans dispatchable to classical computer systems.
concepts.importance: Provides the conceptual framework for the entire second half of the talk, justifying why structured outputs enable fundamentally new application patterns.

concepts.name: Multi-backend RAG with query decomposition
concepts.explanation: RAG systems modeled as Pydantic objects with execute methods that dispatch across multiple search backends (video, email). The search type, title, query, and date filters are all structured fields, enabling polymorphic dispatch and query decomposition.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that structured prompting enables more sophisticated RAG architectures than monolithic retrieval prompts, with type-safe multi-backend support.

concepts.name: Citation-validated question answering
concepts.explanation: A QA pattern where each extracted fact carries a substring quote validated against source text chunks. Validators enforce that quotes exist verbatim in the source, discarding unsupported facts to prevent hallucination programmatically rather than through prompting instructions.
concepts.importance: Provides a concrete, enforceable mechanism for hallucination prevention in retrieval-augmented systems, a critical production concern.

concepts.name: Knowledge graph extraction
concepts.explanation: LLMs extract entities and relationships as structured graph data using ID-reference patterns, producing data structures that mirror graph visualization APIs. Liu demonstrates this achievable in approximately 40 lines of code.
concepts.importance: Shows that structured prompting enables extraction of complex relational knowledge from text, not just flat records, with minimal integration code.

concepts.name: Multimodal structured output
concepts.explanation: Future direction discussed at the talk's conclusion: structured outputs for images and audio, including bounding boxes for object detection and generative UI overlays. This extends typed output contracts beyond text to visual and audio modalities.
concepts.importance: Points to the next frontier of structured prompting, where the same validation and typing patterns extend to non-text modalities.

concepts.name: Max-retries / reasing
concepts.explanation: A feedback loop where validation errors from a failed LLM response are appended to the conversation and re-sent to the model for correction. Liu explicitly distinguishes this from prompt chaining and constitutional AI — it is validation error handling with reasing.
concepts.importance: Transforms validation from a binary pass/fail into an iterative correction mechanism, improving reliability without complex agent architectures.

concepts.name: Instructor library
concepts.explanation: Jason Liu's Python library that patches the OpenAI completion API so callers define a Pydantic model as the response_model parameter and receive guaranteed typed Pydantic object instances. It supports nested models, retries, and streaming. Verified externally as a real library with 13.8K+ GitHub stars, MIT license, and 6M+ monthly downloads.
concepts.importance: The concrete tooling that makes structured prompting practical; it is the bridge between Pydantic type definitions and the OpenAI API.

concepts.name: Pydantic typed data models
concepts.explanation: Pydantic models use Python type hints to define data schemas that automatically parse, validate, and serialize input. In the talk, a Delivery model auto-coerces string timestamps and list-of-strings dimensions into correct Python types, providing IDE autocomplete and spellchecking. This replaces fragile manual JSON parsing.
concepts.importance: Core foundation of the entire talk; every pattern and demonstration builds on Pydantic models as the typed contract between LLMs and Python code.

concepts.name: JSON Schema generation from type hints
concepts.explanation: Pydantic models automatically generate JSON schemas from their type annotations. In the talk, docstrings and field descriptions become part of this schema, unifying code quality, prompt quality, and data quality into a single artifact.
concepts.importance: This is the mechanism that connects Python type definitions to LLM-consumable schemas, eliminating the need to manually write or maintain separate schema files.

concepts.name: Nested model composition
concepts.explanation: Pydantic supports nested models, enabling complex hierarchical data structures. The talk demonstrates UserDetails containing address, BestFriend, and a Friends list referencing UserDetails, enabling extraction of rich, self-referential objects from LLM output.
concepts.importance: Enables modeling real-world domain objects with internal structure, which is essential for extracting anything beyond flat key-value pairs from LLM responses.

concepts.name: Classical field validators
concepts.explanation: Pydantic validators run on model fields to enforce constraints. The talk demonstrates a validator normalizing a string to lowercase and raising a ValidationError on failure, providing programmatic enforcement of data quality rules.
concepts.importance: Provides a code-first mechanism for constraining LLM output that is more reliable than prompt-level instructions alone.

concepts.name: Escape-hatch schema pattern
concepts.explanation: An escape-hatch schema (e.g., MaybeUser) includes optional result, error, and error_message fields, allowing the model to express uncertainty rather than being forced into incorrect answers. This is important for production reliability where models may not always have enough information.
concepts.importance: Addresses a critical production concern: preventing hallucination by giving the model a graceful way to signal it does not know the answer.

concepts.name: Retry-on-validation-error pattern
concepts.explanation: The max-retries mechanism appends validation errors to the conversation history and re-sends to the LLM, enabling automatic self-correction. Liu explicitly distinguishes this from prompt chaining or constitutional AI — it is straightforward validation error handling with reasing.
concepts.importance: Turns validation failures into a feedback loop, dramatically improving reliability without complex agent architectures.

concepts.name: Toggleable chain-of-thought components
concepts.explanation: Reusable Pydantic components like TimeRange include an optional chain-of-thought field that can be enabled during development/testing for transparency and disabled in production to reduce latency. This pattern separates reasoning from output structure.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates how structured prompting enables fine-grained control over model behavior, toggling between observability and performance as needed.

concepts.name: Graph extraction via ID-reference patterns
concepts.explanation: By giving entities unique IDs and storing relationships as lists of IDs (e.g., UserDetails with an id field and a friends list of IDs), LLMs can extract relational graphs and networks from unstructured text. The resulting structure can be traversed programmatically.
concepts.importance: Enables extraction of relational and network data — not just flat records — from unstructured text, opening up graph-based applications.

concepts.name: Polymorphic dispatch via execute methods
concepts.explanation: Pydantic objects can carry execute methods that dispatch to different backends based on their type. The talk demonstrates RAG search objects with search type (email/video), title, query, and before-date fields, each with an execute method routing to the appropriate backend.
concepts.importance: Bridges data modeling and behavior, enabling the LLM to produce not just data but executable plans that integrate with real systems.

concepts.name: DAG-based query planning with dependencies
concepts.explanation: Query plans are modeled as DAG nodes with an ID, question, and dependency list. Independent queries can execute in parallel while dependent queries wait, enabling efficient parallel execution of decomposed complex questions.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that LLMs can output structured plans that classical systems execute, replacing fragile agent loops with deterministic graph traversal.

concepts.name: API-mirroring data structures
concepts.explanation: By designing Pydantic data models to mirror downstream API structures (e.g., graph visualization APIs), integration code is dramatically simplified. The talk demonstrates knowledge graph extraction producing structures directly consumable by visualization tools in ~40 lines of code.
concepts.importance: Shows that thoughtful data model design reduces integration friction, a key software engineering principle applied to LLM outputs.

concepts.name: Substring citation validation
concepts.explanation: In the QA demonstration, each fact carries a substring quote that is validated against source text chunks. Validators discard any fact whose quote is not found verbatim in the source, preventing hallucination programmatically rather than through prompting alone.
concepts.importance: Provides a concrete, code-enforced mechanism for grounding LLM outputs in source material, a critical concern for production retrieval systems.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Liu introduces structured prompting with type hints and Pydantic, noting that LLMs are eating software and 90% of production applications involve asking models for JSON output parsed with regex. The goal is backwards compatibility with existing systems via schemas and APIs.

sections.title: The JSON Reliability Problem
sections.summary: Illustrates common failure modes: threatening models for JSON, models prepending conversational text, inconsistent key names, and the fragility of string pipelines even with OpenAI function calling, which still requires json.loads and leaves developers with unsafe dictionaries.

sections.title: Pydantic as the Solution
sections.summary: Introduces Pydantic as a widely-trusted validation library (70M monthly downloads) powered by type hints. Demonstrates a Delivery model that auto-parses string timestamps and list dimensions, giving IDE autocomplete and spellchecking. Structured prompting means prompts are code, not triple-quoted strings.

sections.title: Instructor Library and Marvin
sections.summary: Presents Instructor, which patches OpenAI's completion API so a Pydantic model set as response_model guarantees typed output. Mentions Marvin as a more comprehensive alternative supporting additional LLMs. Highlights nested references, methods on models, and returning instances instead of dictionaries.

sections.title: Docstrings, Validators, and Retries
sections.summary: Explains that docstrings and field descriptions become part of the JSON schema, unifying code, prompt, and data quality. Demonstrates classical validators and LLM validators. Introduces max-retries for feeding validation errors back to the model for reasing—distinct from prompt chaining or constitutional AI.

sections.title: Design Patterns: Escape Hatches, Reusability, and Graphs
sections.summary: Showcases escape-hatch schemas (MaybeUser with optional result/error) for uncertainty, reusable TimeRange components with toggleable chain-of-thought fields, property extraction with index-based counting limits, and network extraction using IDs with friends lists to pull relational graphs from unstructured text.

sections.title: Advanced Applications: RAG, Query Planning, and Citation Validation
sections.summary: Frames structured prompting as the C-to-C++ shift—object-oriented development for LLMs enabling models to output traversable data structures. Demonstrates RAG with multiple search backends modeled as Pydantic objects with execute methods, query planning as a DAG with dependencies for parallel execution, knowledge graph extraction mirroring visualization APIs in ~40 lines, and citation-validated QA where facts carry substring quotes validated against source text to prevent hallucination programmatically.

sections.title: Future Directions and Conclusion
sections.summary: Discusses future multimodal structured outputs including bounding boxes for images enabling generative UI, structured evaluation tooling for comparing response distributions, and references instructor at jxnl.github.io. Emphasizes that creativity in prompting these systems will be the limiting factor as models improve, and the discipline shifts from prompt engineering toward domain modeling.

organization.name: 567 Labs
organization.summary: 567 Labs (also known as 567 Studios, formerly Fivesixseven LLC) is Jason Liu's AI consulting and open-source development company. At the time of the AI Engineer Summit 2023 talk, the entity was known as Fivesixseven LLC and was listed as Jason Liu's affiliation on the speaker page. The company provided AI consulting services to clients including Zapier, HubSpot, Weights & Biases, Modal Labs, Timescale, and Pydantic. It also ran cohort-based RAG training programs with students from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and Amazon. The consulting practice was subsequently closed after Jason Liu joined OpenAI as a Developer Experience Engineer on the Codex team.
organization.status: Consulting practice closed. Jason Liu now employed at OpenAI as Developer Experience Engineer on Codex team. Instructor library remains active as open-source project with 6M+ monthly downloads and 11k+ GitHub stars.

technologies.label: Pydantic typed data validation
technologies.summary: Pydantic is the foundational technology of the entire talk. Liu argues that Pydantic — a widely-trusted Python data validation library with 70M monthly downloads — should be the bridge between LLM function calling and typed Python code. Pydantic models use type hints to define data schemas that automatically parse, validate, and serialize input, provide IDE autocomplete, and generate JSON schemas from their annotations. The talk demonstrates that docstrings and field descriptions become part of the JSON schema, unifying code quality, prompt quality, and data quality into a single maintainable artifact. Every advanced pattern in the talk — validators, escape-hatches, graph extraction, DAG query planning, citation-validated QA, API-mirroring — is built on Pydantic models as the typed contract. Liu frames this as the C-to-C++ shift for LLM systems: object-oriented development where LLMs output traversable data structures that classical systems process.
technologies.role: Core foundation — every pattern, demonstration, and design principle in the talk is built on Pydantic typed data models as the contract between LLM output and Python code

technologies.label: Instructor structured output extraction
technologies.summary: Instructor is the primary tooling that makes structured prompting practical. Created by the speaker Jason Liu, it patches the OpenAI completion API so callers define a Pydantic model as the response_model parameter and receive guaranteed typed Pydantic object instances. Key features demonstrated include nested model support, methods on returned instances (not raw dictionaries), and the max-retries pattern that feeds validation errors back to the model for automatic self-correction. Liu explicitly distinguishes max-retries from prompt chaining and constitutional AI — it is validation error handling with reasing. At the time of the talk, Instructor only worked with OpenAI function calling; it has since expanded to support 15+ LLM providers. OpenAI cited Instructor as one of five open-source libraries that inspired their Structured Outputs API feature announced August 2024.
technologies.role: Primary tool — the library that patches OpenAI's API to guarantee Pydantic-typed responses, demonstrated with nested models, retries, and streaming throughout the talk

technologies.label: OpenAI function calling API
technologies.summary: OpenAI function calling is the API protocol underlying the entire structured prompting approach. Released in June 2023, it improves JSON placement in model responses but still yields raw dictionaries requiring json.loads, leaving developers with unsafe untyped data. Liu positions function calling as a necessary but insufficient step — Instructor patches it to deliver guaranteed typed Pydantic objects. The talk's temporal context is significant: at the time of presentation (October 2023), function calling was the primary mechanism for structured output, and the dedicated Structured Outputs API would not arrive until August 2024. OpenAI's Structured Outputs announcement explicitly acknowledged Instructor as inspiration, validating the talk's thesis post-hoc.
technologies.role: Underlying API mechanism — the function calling protocol that Instructor patches to guarantee typed Pydantic responses; noted as improving JSON placement but insufficient without typed validation

technologies.label: Marvin structured output framework
technologies.summary: Marvin is mentioned in the talk as a more comprehensive alternative to Instructor, supporting additional LLMs beyond OpenAI. Liu notes that Instructor only works with OpenAI function calling and that Marvin is needed for broader LLM support. Marvin is a Python framework by PrefectHQ for producing structured outputs and building agentic AI workflows using Pydantic models. Since the talk, Marvin has evolved significantly: Marvin 3.0 merged with ControlFlow and now uses Pydantic AI for LLM interactions, supporting the full range of LLM providers that Pydantic AI supports. The mention is brief but notable because it frames the ecosystem of Pydantic-based structured output libraries and acknowledges the OpenAI-only limitation of Instructor at the time.
technologies.role: Mentioned as a broader alternative to Instructor for LLM support beyond OpenAI — addresses the key limitation of Instructor at the time of the talk

evidence.excerpt: 90% of the applications you build are just ones when you're asking a language model to Output Json
evidence.supports: Most production LLM apps are structured output extraction problems

evidence.excerpt: pantic is a library that do data model validation very similar to data classes it is powered by typ pints
evidence.supports: Pydantic provides data validation similar to dataclasses, powered by type hints

evidence.excerpt: it is has really great model and field validation it has 70 million downloads a month
evidence.supports: Pydantic has 70 million monthly downloads indicating trust and maintenance

evidence.excerpt: Define your pantic object you set that as the response model of that create call and now you're guaranteed that that response model is the type of the entity that you extract
evidence.supports: Instructor patches OpenAI API to return guaranteed Pydantic-typed objects

evidence.excerpt: this isn't like prompt chain this is this isn't constitutional AI here we just have validation error handling and then reasing
evidence.supports: Max-retries pattern is validation error handling, not prompt chaining or constitutional AI

evidence.excerpt: it's really important for us to give language models the ability to have an escape hatch and say that it doesn't know something
evidence.supports: Escape-hatch schemas let models express uncertainty rather than forcing string-matching

evidence.excerpt: when we go from C to C++ the thing we get is object oriented programming and that makes a lot of things easier
evidence.supports: Structured prompting is analogous to the shift from C to C++ object-oriented programming

evidence.excerpt: they can represent you know knowledge workflows and even plans that you can just dispatch to a classical computer
evidence.supports: LLMs can output data structures representing knowledge, workflows, and plans dispatchable to classical systems

evidence.excerpt: the search type is email or video search has a title a query a before dat and a type and then you can just implement the execute method
evidence.supports: RAG searches modeled as Pydantic objects with execute methods for multi-backend dispatch

evidence.excerpt: if I'm good at Elite code I could query the first two in parallel because there are no dependencies and then wait for dependency three to merge
evidence.supports: DAG query planning enables parallel execution of independent queries with dependency-aware merging

evidence.excerpt: for every quote you give me validate that it exists in the text Chunk if it's not there throw out the fact
evidence.supports: Citation validators enforce that fact quotes exist as substrings in source text to prevent hallucination
